transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

I've come in because my eating has been really off for months. Some days I barely eat—just toast and coffee—and other days I'll buy a bunch of sweets at the bakery even though I don't really enjoy them.
When you eat those sweets at the bakery, do you feel like you can't stop or control how much you're eating once you start?
I'm not really sure. I do buy more than I mean to sometimes, but I haven't paid much attention to whether I can't stop once I start eating them.
After you eat those sweets, do you ever try to get rid of the calories—like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising a lot to compensate?
I haven't really thought about it that way. I don't know—I haven't noticed myself doing anything specifically after I eat them.
When you're eating very little on those days, is it because you're trying to control your weight or shape, or do you just not feel hungry or interested in food?
It’s not really about my weight. My eating has just gotten turned around—some days I only pick at toast and coffee, and other days I’m standing in the bakery buying sweets I don’t even enjoy.
Over these past months, have you also noticed feeling persistently sad, low, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?
Yeah. Most mornings I wake up with this heavy sadness already on me. Even when I’m in my bright kitchen making coffee, it just feels like the warmth has gone out of everything.
How long have you been feeling this way—waking up with that heavy sadness and feeling like the warmth has gone out of things?
About seven months now—since my aunt came to live with me after her fall.
Besides the sadness, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities or things you used to enjoy over these past several months?

Yes. I used to get excited about quilting squares, bowling night, planning potlucks—things like that. Now I look at my supplies or the church calendar and I just... can’t make myself care the way I used to.
Along with the sadness and loss of interest, have you noticed changes in your sleep or energy levels—like trouble sleeping, sleeping too much, or feeling unusually tired most days?
Even when I get a full night without my aunt calling out, I’m worn down by breakfast. Carrying laundry or making a few phone calls takes more out of me than it feels like it should.
Over these past several months, have you found yourself feeling unusually guilty, worthless, or overly critical of yourself?

I do. Even when people at church tell me I’m doing fine, I can’t shake the feeling that everyone in Manawa knows I’m letting my aunt down. Like they’re whispering about me, about what a burden I’ve become.
When you say you feel like people are whispering about you being a burden, do you actually hear them saying these things, or is it more a strong feeling or belief you have even without any evidence?
I don’t actually hear voices saying it. It’s more that I just know they’re talking, even when they smile and tell me I’m doing fine. Everybody in Manawa must see what a burden I’ve become to my aunt.

When people reassure you and there's no real evidence anyone is talking about you, are you still completely convinced they are—unable to be talked out of it—or can you consider that it might not be true?
I mean, I know they say it isn’t true, but I can’t really believe them. It feels like everybody in Manawa can see I’m letting my aunt down, and they’re talking about what a burden I am.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a single depressive episode of ~7 months duration marked by depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue/low energy, and feelings of worthlessness/guilt, meeting core and associated criteria for major depressive disorder. In addition, she holds a fixed, near-delusional belief that the community is talking about her being a burden, which persists despite reassurance and contrary evidence, indicating mood-congruent psychotic features (no true auditory hallucinations, but a delusional level of conviction). The disordered eating pattern (skipping meals vs. impulsive sweet buying) appears secondary to the depressive episode rather than meeting criteria for a primary eating disorder, as there is no clear binge-eating loss of control, compensatory behavior, or weight/shape concern reported. This supports a diagnosis of severe major depressive episode with psychotic features over an eating disorder or non-psychotic severe depression.
